title: Longest Arithmetic Progression
statement:
You are given an array of `n` integers. Find the length of the longest **arithmetic progression** that can be obtained as a subsequence of the array.

A subsequence keeps the original left-to-right order of the chosen elements but may skip elements; the elements do not need to be adjacent. A sequence is an arithmetic progression if the difference between every two consecutive elements is the same constant (which may be zero or negative). A sequence of one or two elements is always an arithmetic progression.

For example, in `[20, 1, 15, 3, 10, 5, 8]` the subsequence `20, 15, 10, 5` has common difference `-5`.
inputFormat:
The first line contains `n`.
The second line contains `n` integers.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the length of the longest arithmetic progression subsequence.

examples.explanation: The whole array is an arithmetic progression with difference 3.
The subsequence 4, 7, 10 has difference 3 and uses positions 1, 2 and 4. No arithmetic subsequence of length 4 exists.
The subsequence 20, 15, 10, 5 (positions 0, 2, 4, 5) has difference -5 and is the longest.

hints: Fix the last element of the progression and its common difference. What do you need to know about the progression that ends one step earlier?

Let f[j][d] be the length of the longest arithmetic subsequence ending at index j with common difference d. For every i < j, set d = nums[j] - nums[i] and extend f[i][d], or start a new pair of length 2 if f[i][d] does not exist.
The differences can be as large as 2 * 10^9, so store f[j] in a hash map keyed by d instead of a 2D array. The answer is the largest value stored anywhere (and at least 1).
